Using the neutr package

Source: vignettes/Using-the-neutr-package.Rmd
Using-the-neutr-package.Rmd
library(neutr)

The neutr package does two things for neutral models of species assemblages:

  • inference: maximum likelihood estimation of the parameters of the Ewens model (optim_ewens()), the Etienne model of a local community with dispersal limitation (optim_etienne()), the Pitman model (optim_pitman()) and the multideme model (optim_multideme());
  • generation: fast and exact simulation of typical species abundance distributions of the Ewens model (generate_hoppe_urn0(), generate_hoppe_urn()) and of the Pitman model (generate_pitman_urn()), including for samples of 101210^{12} individuals and more.

A species abundance distribution is a vector of positive counts (n1,…,nk)(n_1, \dots, n_k): kk species, J=∑iniJ = \sum_i n_i individuals.

Generating a community

Ewens’ model has a single parameter θ\theta (the fundamental biodiversity number). generate_hoppe_urn() returns the abundances, sorted in decreasing order, together with the expected number of species for these parameters:

set.seed(42)
com <- generate_hoppe_urn(theta = 11.3, J = 234373)
length(com$abundance)   # species in this draw
#> [1] 109
com$k                   # expected number of species
#> [1] 112.8284
head(com$abundance)
#> [1] 19417 18729 17430 15007 14371 13308
sum(com$abundance)      # always exactly J
#> [1] 234373
plot(com$abundance, log = "y", xlab = "Rank", ylab = "Abundance", pch = 16, cex = 0.6)

Rank-abundance curve of the simulated community.

The generator works with the Griffiths-Engen-McCloskey representation of the model, so its cost hardly depends on the number of individuals:

huge <- generate_hoppe_urn(theta = 100, J = 1e12)
length(huge$abundance)
#> [1] 2339
sum(huge$abundance) == 1e12
#> [1] TRUE

generate_hoppe_urn0() simulates Hoppe’s urn exactly, individual by individual (vectorised, so still fast for samples of millions). It is mostly useful as a reference. It draws random numbers with the dqrng package, which has its own random stream: set.seed() does not affect it, use its seed argument:

a <- generate_hoppe_urn0(theta = 11.3, J = 1e5, seed = 1)
b <- generate_hoppe_urn0(theta = 11.3, J = 1e5, seed = 1)
identical(a, b)
#> [1] TRUE

The Pitman model adds a discount parameter σ∈(0,1)\sigma \in (0, 1), which gives heavier tails (more rare species) than Ewens’ model:

set.seed(1)
pit <- generate_pitman_urn(theta = 10, sigma = 0.3, J = 1e5)
c(species = length(pit$abundance), expected = round(pit$k, 1))
#>  species expected 
#>    415.0    500.6

Estimating the parameters

optim_ewens() gives the maximum likelihood estimate of θ\theta, which solves k=θ[ψ(θ+J)−ψ(θ)]k = \theta[\psi(\theta + J) - \psi(\theta)]:

ab <- c(234, 87, 34, 5, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1)
ew <- optim_ewens(ab)
ew
#> $theta
#> [1] 2.476993
#> 
#> $logl
#> [1] -433.6187

optim_pitman() estimates (θ,σ)(\theta, \sigma):

pm <- optim_pitman(ab, init_vals = c(10, 0.1))
pm
#> $theta
#> [1] 0.7110667
#> 
#> $sigma
#> [1] 0.2781073
#> 
#> $logl
#> [1] -432.4741
#> 
#> $converged
#> [1] TRUE

Comparing the two models

The Ewens model is the Pitman model with σ=0\sigma = 0, so the two are nested and can be compared with a likelihood-ratio test or AIC. The logl element returned by optim_ewens() and optim_pitman() is on the same scale for both functions:

lrt <- 2 * (pm$logl - ew$logl)
c(LRT = lrt, p.value = pchisq(lrt, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
#>       LRT   p.value 
#> 2.2893221 0.1302668
c(Ewens = -2 * ew$logl + 2 * 1, Pitman = -2 * pm$logl + 2 * 2)   # AIC
#>    Ewens   Pitman 
#> 869.2374 868.9481

(As σ=0\sigma = 0 lies on the boundary of the parameter space, the χ12\chi^2_1 p-value is conservative; halve it for the usual boundary correction.)

Recovering known parameters 

set.seed(2024)
sim <- generate_pitman_urn(theta = 10, sigma = 0.3, J = 1e5)$abundance
fit <- optim_pitman(sim)
round(c(theta = fit$theta, sigma = fit$sigma), 3)   # truth: 10 and 0.3
#>  theta  sigma 
#> 14.626  0.267

Boundary estimates

When the likelihood has no interior maximum for the data at hand, the estimate lands on the edge of the search interval and the functions issue a warning:

tryCatch(optim_ewens(rep(1, 20)), warning = function(w) conditionMessage(w))
#> [1] "optim_ewens(): every species has a single individual; the likelihood increases with theta without bound (estimate: Inf)."

A local community with dispersal limitation: the Etienne model

In Etienne’s (2005) model, a local community of J individuals receives immigrants from a neutral metacommunity with fundamental biodiversity number θ\theta, at rate mm. optim_etienne() estimates (θ,m)(\theta, m) from a single sample; on the example of Etienne’s paper it reproduces his estimates θ=7.05\theta = 7.05 and m=0.226m = 0.226:

zoo <- c(8, 5, 3, 2, 1, 1)
et <- optim_etienne(zoo)
et
#> $theta
#> [1] 7.047969
#> 
#> $m
#> [1] 0.2263591
#> 
#> $I
#> [1] 5.559197
#> 
#> $logl
#> [1] -28.56215
#> 
#> $converged
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $se_theta
#> [1] 15.10683
#> 
#> $se_m
#> [1] 0.3349456
#> 
#> $se_I
#> [1] 10.63283
#> 
#> $local_maxima
#>      theta         m        I      logl boundary
#> 1 7.047969 0.2263591 5.559197 -28.56215    FALSE

The model with m=1m = 1 (no dispersal limitation) is the Ewens model, and the logl values of the two functions are on the same scale:

ew_zoo <- optim_ewens(zoo)
lrt <- 2 * (et$logl - ew_zoo$logl)
c(LRT = lrt, p.value = pchisq(lrt, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE))
#>       LRT   p.value 
#> 0.3577858 0.5497385

(As for the Pitman model, m=1m = 1 lies on the boundary of the parameter space and the χ12\chi^2_1 p-value is conservative.) When the data show no dispersal limitation, the estimate of mm reaches its upper bound, with a warning, and the Etienne model reduces to the Ewens model; this is the case for the sample ab used above:

suppressWarnings(optim_etienne(ab))[c("theta", "m", "logl")]
#> $theta
#> [1] 2.476993
#> 
#> $m
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $logl
#> [1] -433.6187
ew_ab <- optim_ewens(ab)
ew_ab
#> $theta
#> [1] 2.476993
#> 
#> $logl
#> [1] -433.6187

The likelihood itself is given by logl_etienne(). It depends on the data through the coefficients K(D,A)K(D,A), which are the expensive part of the calculation (their cost grows as J2J^2): compute them once with logkda() to evaluate the likelihood many times, for instance along a profile:

lk <- logkda(zoo)
m <- seq(0.02, 1, by = 0.01)
plot(m, logl_etienne(zoo, et$theta, m, log_kda = lk), type = "l",
     xlab = "immigration rate m", ylab = "log-likelihood")
abline(v = et$m, lty = 2)

Profile of the log-likelihood in m, at the estimated theta.

Uncertainty and local maxima

optim_etienne() returns standard errors (se_theta, se_m, se_I) from the inverse Hessian, and with ci = TRUE likelihood-ratio confidence intervals, which are preferable because the likelihood is often strongly asymmetric. A limit equal to a bound of the search interval means that the interval extends at least that far:

fit <- optim_etienne(zoo, ci = TRUE)
rbind(theta = c(estimate = fit$theta, se = fit$se_theta, fit$ci_theta),
      m     = c(estimate = fit$m,     se = fit$se_m,     fit$ci_m))
#>        estimate         se      lower upper
#> theta 7.0479694 15.1068324 0.81149497  2000
#> m     0.2263591  0.3349456 0.04102535     1

The likelihood surface can have several local maxima; all those found are listed in local_maxima, the global one first:

optim_etienne(c(15, 81, 80, 2, 1, 2))$local_maxima
#>       theta           m          I      logl boundary
#> 1 21.747365 0.006867291    1.24466 -195.2637    FALSE
#> 2  1.056303 0.980993441 9290.41505 -195.2851    FALSE

Data files of the TeTame software

The TeTame software (Chave and Jabot) reads species abundances from a text file, one value per line, samples being separated by a line containing &. Such a file is easily read in R. Here we write the trial file distributed with TeTame 2.1:

file <- tempfile(fileext = ".txt")
writeLines(c(1, 8, 80, 2, 1, 20, 0, "&", 15, 8, 8, 20, 10, 2, 0, "&",
             15, 81, 80, 2, 1, 2, 0), file)

x <- scan(file, what = "", quiet = TRUE)
samples <- unname(split(as.numeric(x[x != "&"]), cumsum(x == "&")[x != "&"]))

TeTame’s option e estimates (θ,m)(\theta, m) in each sample. TeTame reports the negative log-probability of the abundance vector, which is -logl_etienne(..., full = TRUE):

do.call(rbind, lapply(samples, function(y) {
  fit <- suppressWarnings(optim_etienne(y))
  data.frame(S = length(y[y > 0]), J = sum(y), theta = fit$theta, se_theta = fit$se_theta,
             m = fit$m, se_m = fit$se_m,
             negloglik = -logl_etienne(y, fit$theta, fit$m, full = TRUE),
             n_local_maxima = nrow(fit$local_maxima))
}))
#>   S   J     theta   se_theta           m        se_m negloglik n_local_maxima
#> 1 6 112  1.195285         NA 0.999999990          NA  10.77968              2
#> 2 6  63  2.947770   2.582702 0.102035222 0.120382867  12.22751              1
#> 3 6 181 21.747365 110.037756 0.006867291 0.006534417  13.53646              2

TeTame’s option j (Jabot et al. 2008) estimates mm in each sample, the regional pool being the sum of the samples: this is optim_multideme(), with one row per sample (the species must be in the same order in every sample):

optim_multideme(do.call(rbind, samples), ci = TRUE)[c("I", "se_I", "m", "se_m", "ci_m")]
#> $I
#> [1]  7.419698  5.738001 14.671141
#> 
#> $se_I
#> [1] 4.337811 3.235172 9.373103
#> 
#> $m
#> [1] 0.06265594 0.08470874 0.07536372
#> 
#> $se_m
#> [1] 0.03433568 0.04371438 0.04451975
#> 
#> $ci_m
#>           lower     upper
#> [1,] 0.01858430 0.1636401
#> [2,] 0.02650112 0.2057232
#> [3,] 0.02043186 0.2125176

The likelihood surface is computed on a grid with logl_etienne(), which is vectorised; the contour delimits the joint 95% confidence region:

y <- samples[[2]]
fit <- optim_etienne(y)
lk <- logkda(y)                                  # computed once for the whole grid
grid <- expand.grid(theta = exp(seq(log(0.5), log(200), length.out = 80)),
                    m = seq(0.005, 1, length.out = 80))
grid$logl <- logl_etienne(y, grid$theta, grid$m, log_kda = lk)
z <- matrix(grid$logl - fit$logl, 80, 80)
image(log(unique(grid$theta)), unique(grid$m), pmax(z, -10), col = hcl.colors(50),
      xlab = "log(theta)", ylab = "m")
contour(log(unique(grid$theta)), unique(grid$m), z, levels = -qchisq(0.95, 2) / 2,
        drawlabels = FALSE, add = TRUE)
points(log(fit$theta), fit$m, pch = 19)

Log-likelihood surface of the second sample of the TeTame trial file; the contour delimits the joint 95% confidence region and the point is the maximum likelihood estimate.

The multideme model

optim_multideme() takes a matrix with one row per deme (local community) and one column per species. The regional abundance distribution is the sum of the rows. For each deme it estimates the rescaled immigration rate I=m1−m(J−1)I = \frac{m}{1 - m}(J - 1) and the immigration rate mm:

demes <- rbind(
  c(44, 37, 34, 5, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1),
  c(240, 20, 48, 2, 21, 1, 3, 2, 5, 2, 0, 1, 1)
)
optim_multideme(demes)
#> $I
#> [1]  69.44552 197.91949
#> 
#> $m
#> [1] 0.3363867 0.3645467
#> 
#> $J
#> [1] 138 346
#> 
#> $k
#> [1] 13 12
#> 
#> $logl
#> [1] -255.5496 -392.8408
#> 
#> $se_I
#> [1]  34.80389 128.98987
#> 
#> $se_m
#> [1] 0.1118761 0.1509746

Use verbose = TRUE to follow the progress over many demes.

Expected number of species

kest() is the exact expected number of species in the Ewens model. kest_gt() and kest_gt0() give the expected number of species with more than N individuals, deterministically (an approximation, via an integral) and by simulation:

kest(11.3, 234373)
#> [1] 112.8284
kest_gt(11.3, 234373, N = 50)$value
#> [1] 62.12428
set.seed(3)
kest_gt0(11.3, 234373, N = 50, nrep = 50)
#> $k
#> [1] 62.5
#> 
#> $sigmak
#> [1] 7.349163
